title: What Does ‘Where Two or Three Are Gathered’ Really Mean?
subtitle: Jesus made this promise while teaching his disciples what to do when a brother sins against them. It belongs to the church's hardest room, not only its emptiest one.

sections.title: A Promise for Small Rooms
sections.body:
“For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them” (Matthew 18:20). Many of us learned it in older words, where two or three are gathered, and most of us meet it in small rooms. It's said at the start of a prayer meeting when half the chairs are empty, around a hospital bed where three people have joined hands, at a kitchen table where a Bible study has dwindled to a faithful few. It's the verse people reach for when the attendance is disappointing and the faith isn't.

There are good reasons to love it. A church that measures itself by counting heads can make its most faithful people feel like failures, and this verse says the Lord of the church doesn't count the way we do. It gives weight to the smallest gathering and dignity to the people who keep coming after others have stopped. Whoever has prayed with two friends in a waiting room and sensed they weren't alone was not imagining things.

The skeptic has noticed something else, and he's right about it. Christians sometimes say this verse as a consolation prize for a thin crowd, and sometimes as a formula, as though Jesus needed a quorum before he would come. Said that way, it quietly suggests that the believer who prays alone gets less of him. We've asked the verse to do strange work.

It can hold the comfort people bring to it. But Jesus didn't first say it about a prayer meeting. He said it in the middle of instructions for what to do when a brother sins against you, and that changes what kind of comfort it is.

sections.title: Between the Lost Sheep and the Forgiven Debt
sections.body:
The Gospel doesn't name its author. Early tradition connects it with Matthew, one of the Twelve, and most scholars date it to the second half of the first century. It gathers Jesus' teaching into five long discourses, and chapter 18, the fourth, concerns life among his disciples.

The scene is Capernaum (17:24). Jesus has just told the disciples, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men” (Matthew 17:22), and they are deeply grieved. Their next question is “Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” (Matthew 18:1). Jesus answers by inviting a little child to stand among them. He warns that whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble would be better off drowned with a millstone around his neck (18:6), and tells of a man who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one that strayed: “your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish” (Matthew 18:14).

Our verse's paragraph follows. “If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over” (Matthew 18:15). If he won't listen, take one or two others along, because the law said, “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). If he refuses them, tell it to the church, a word no other Gospel uses, and if he refuses the church, “regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector” (Matthew 18:17). The power to bind and loose, promised to Peter in 16:19, is now spoken to the disciples together (18:18) and lands on the church's decision about that brother. Two who agree in prayer are promised the Father's answer (18:19), and then comes our verse.

Right after it, Peter asks how often he must forgive a brother, “Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). Jesus says seventy-seven, and tells of a servant forgiven a debt he could never repay who then had a fellow servant thrown into prison over a small one. The chapter ends with a warning to forgive “your brother from your heart” (Matthew 18:35).

sections.title: Who the Two or Three Were
sections.body:
Read in its paragraph, the numbers in verse 20 aren't casual. Two or three is the count of witnesses the law required, and it's exactly the company verse 16 describes: the disciple who was wronged, with the one or two who went along. In context, the two who agree in verse 19 most naturally belong to that company, and their request concerns, first of all, the brother who hasn't listened yet. Verse 20 even begins with “For”; the promise explains what comes before it.

Think what that meant to men who would soon have to deal with one another's sins without him in the room. The church Matthew wrote for had no courts and no way to compel anyone; the only sanction it had was withdrawing its fellowship. Jesus tells people in that position that what they bind on earth is bound in heaven, that the Father hears the two who agree, and that he himself will be among them.

That last promise is larger than it sounds. A rabbinic saying later preserved in the Mishnah holds that when two sit together and words of the law pass between them, God's presence rests among them. Jesus puts himself where that saying puts the presence of God. Matthew's Gospel opens with a child called Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), and closes with “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). This verse stands between them, in the room where the church does its hardest work.

Even the last step bears his mark. The brother who won't listen is to be treated as an outsider, and the words mean that. But Matthew's readers knew how Jesus treated outsiders. He called a tax collector from his booth and ate with many more (9:9-10), and the Gospel that carries that man's name lists him among the Twelve as “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3). Put outside, he becomes the kind of person Jesus went looking for.

sections.title: What It Promises, and What It Doesn't
sections.body:
Of the verses in this series, this one reaches us with the fewest detours, since Jesus is already speaking about the church (18:17). So it still promises what it promised then. When believers take up the costly work of restoring one another, Christ is among them. The one who goes privately to a brother, the witnesses who go along, and the church that finally has to decide aren't alone, and they don't act on their own authority either.

What it doesn't promise matters as much. Two or three was the number the law required for testimony, never a quorum for his presence. The Father sees the one who prays behind a shut door (6:6), and the risen Christ is with his people always, so the small prayer meeting is right to take comfort in him, and so is the believer praying alone.

Nor does the verse make agreement a way to corner God. Some prosperity teaching, wanting to take Jesus at his word, treats verse 19 as a technique, as if two believers agreeing on a healing or a house could bind heaven to deliver it. The skeptic who hears magic in that hears correctly. The heaven-and-earth language of verses 18 and 19 echoes the prayer Jesus taught: “Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). A church binds and looses as people who have prayed that prayer. In Gethsemane, with three disciples nearby, the Son himself prayed, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39).

The phrase “in My name” (18:20) isn't a banner either. Gatherings on the right and on the left have claimed his presence for their cause, as though his name could be stamped onto a meeting already planned. To gather in his name is to put the gathering under his authority, including his authority to rebuke it. I'm a pastor, and I know how much easier it is to quote this verse over a meeting than to let it govern one.

sections.title: The Room Where He Promised to Be
sections.body:
Keep saying it when half the chairs are empty; it's true there. But practice it where Jesus put it. When someone sins against you, go to him privately before saying a word about him to anyone else. Go having first taken “the beam out of your own eye” (Matthew 7:5), and go hoping to win your brother over. Leviticus made the choice plain: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:17). The quiet alternative to that conversation is a grudge. Churches fail here both ways: some never go to anyone and call it kindness, and others expel quickly to protect their name. Neither goes after the one sheep.

The chapter must also be guarded from its worst misuse. Matthew 18 is not a rule that makes a harmed person meet the one who harmed them. It opens by placing Christ's presence in a child, “whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me” (Matthew 18:5), and by warning of the millstone. Nothing in it asks a child, or anyone who is afraid, to go alone to the person who hurt them. The law behind the two or three witnesses sends a disputed case to judges who “shall investigate thoroughly” (Deuteronomy 19:18), so it's no excuse for refusing to look. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). Forgiving from the heart is not the same as trusting again, reconciling, or keeping quiet. If someone has harmed you, tell someone safe, and if a crime was committed, go to the police. You don't need anyone's permission to be safe.

We've loved this verse in small rooms, and he is there. But he gave it for the hard room: a sinner going to a brother with the truth, two or three praying over a wound they can't close, a church deciding with trembling what to bind and what to loose. The one standing among them is the one whose blood was “poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28), and everyone in that room came in as the servant with a debt too large to pay. Forgiven debtors are all he has ever sent to find a brother.
